# Why the League of Nations could not have prevented the Second World War

The Lamb from the Slaughter. (1919). Library of Congress, Item No. LC-DIG-acd-2a06165. Public Domain. Source: https://www.loc.gov/item/2016678758/

 On 19 November 1919, the United States Senate rejected the Treaty of Versailles and, with it, American membership of the League of Nations: the very organisation that President Woodrow Wilson had designed to guarantee collective security after the First World War. 

 The League had been founded on the principle that member states would protect one another against aggression, yet the absence of the world's largest economy left the organisation without a critical source of military and economic authority from the day it opened its doors in Geneva in January 1920. 

 The League's structural flaws and its failures in Manchuria and Abyssinia makes it obvious that the organisation was never capable of preventing the Second World War. 

## An organisation built on shaky foundations

 Since Woodrow Wilson first proposed the League at the Paris Peace Conference in January 1919, the idea of collective security had depended on one essential assumption: that all major powers would commit to defending the international order. 

 Article 10 of the League's Covenant required members to respect and preserve the territorial integrity of all member states, and Article 16 stated that any member resorting to war in violation of the Covenant would be considered to have committed an act of war against every other member. 

 In theory, this system of automatic sanctions and collective military response was supposed to deter aggression before it began. 

 The Covenant was a short document of twenty-six articles, adopted unanimously at the Paris Peace Conference on 28 April 1919, and it expressed an optimistic belief that rational governments would always prefer negotiation to war. 

 In practice, however, the system had a fatal weakness because the League's Council required a unanimous vote to recommend sanctions or military action. 

 Any single member could therefore block collective action, which meant that the organisation depended entirely on the political will of governments that often had competing interests. 

 Britain and France, the League's two most important members, were frequently reluctant to confront aggressors because they feared provoking a war they were not prepared to fight. 

 As the world's largest economy and most powerful industrial nation, the United States was the very country whose participation would have made the threat of sanctions credible, and its absence from the organisation weakened collective security from the outset. 

 Senator Henry Cabot Lodge had led the opposition to the Treaty in 1919, arguing that Article 10 would oblige the United States to send troops overseas without the approval of Congress. 

 Lodge proposed fourteen reservations to the Treaty. Wilson had suffered a debilitating stroke in October 1919 and was unwilling to accept any compromise. 

 The Treaty was voted down, and the United States never joined the League. 

 Without American economic power and military resources behind the threat of enforcement, the entire system lacked credibility.

## The Manchurian crisis proved that the League could not stop aggression

 On 18 September 1931, officers of the Japanese Kwantung Army staged an explosion on the South Manchurian Railway near Mukden and blamed it on Chinese saboteurs. 

 The damage was minimal, yet the army used the incident to justify a full military occupation of Manchuria over the following weeks. 

 Japanese forces captured towns and railway hubs without formal orders from Tokyo, and the civilian government in Japan proved unable to restrain the military. 

 By March 1932, Japanese authorities had declared the creation of Manchukuo, a puppet state under the nominal rule of Puyi, the former Qing emperor, who had been enticed to Manchuria by Colonel Doihara Kenji, the Kwantung Army's intelligence chief. 

 As soon as the scale of Japan's military operation became clear, China appealed to the League of Nations for assistance. 

 In response, the League appointed a commission led by Lord Lytton, a British diplomat, to investigate the situation. 

 The Lytton Commission spent six weeks in Manchuria in the spring of 1932, interviewing officials and observing military operations. 

 Its report was published in October 1932, in which it concluded that Japan's invasion violated international agreements and that Manchukuo did not possess the characteristics of an independent state. 

 After the League Assembly adopted the Lytton Report on 24 February 1933, with only Japan voting against it, the Japanese delegation walked out of the Assembly and announced the country's withdrawal from the League. 

 No economic sanctions were imposed on Japan because member states, particularly Britain and France, feared the economic consequences and did not want to risk a military confrontation in the Pacific. 

 The Manchurian crisis demonstrated that the League had no way of enforcing its own rulings against a determined aggressor, and it sent a clear message to other expansionist governments that the League would condemn aggression in words but take no meaningful action to stop it. 

 Adolf Hitler and Benito Mussolini both observed Japan's successful defiance of the international order, and both drew the same conclusion: the League could be ignored with impunity. 

## Abyssinia confirmed the League's inability to enforce collective security

 In October 1935, Mussolini ordered the invasion of Abyssinia, an independent African nation that bordered the Italian colony of Eritrea. 

 The Italian dictator wanted to build an overseas empire and avenge Italy's humiliating defeat at the Battle of Adwa in 1896. 

 Emperor Haile Selassie appealed to the League for help, and the organisation condemned Italy as the aggressor. 

 For the first time in its history, the League did impose limited economic sanctions on an aggressor state. 

 It banned arms sales to Italy and prohibited loans to the Italian government. The sanctions, however, did not include oil, the one resource Italy needed most to fuel its military campaign. 

 Member states feared that an oil embargo might provoke Mussolini into declaring war on Britain, and they also worried that the United States, which was not a League member, would simply fill the gap by selling oil to Italy directly. 

 Equally damaging was Britain's refusal to close the Suez Canal to Italian shipping, a decision that allowed Italy to transport troops and supplies freely to East Africa. 

 Behind the scenes, Britain and France actively undermined the League's authority. 

 In December 1935, British Foreign Secretary Samuel Hoare and French Prime Minister Pierre Laval secretly negotiated the Hoare-Laval Pact, which proposed giving two-thirds of Abyssinia to Italy. 

 When the details of the plan were leaked to the press, public outrage in Britain forced Hoare to resign, and the pact was abandoned. 

 The damage to the League's credibility was irreversible. Italy completed its conquest of Abyssinia by May 1936, and Mussolini withdrew Italy from the League in 1937. 

 The historian A. J. P. Taylor later argued that the Hoare-Laval Pact was the event that killed the League of Nations.

## Why no version of the League could have stopped Hitler

 By the time Adolf Hitler remilitarised the Rhineland in March 1936, the League had already lost Japan and was about to lose Italy. 

 Germany had withdrawn in October 1933, shortly after Hitler became Chancellor. 

 The Soviet Union had joined in 1934 but was expelled in December 1939 for invading Finland. 

 The organisation's membership was shrinking at the very moment when the threat of war was growing. 

 Even if the United States had joined the League and the organisation had possessed greater enforcement powers, it is difficult to see how collective security could have contained Nazi Germany. 

 Hitler's foreign policy was driven by a willingness to accept risks that no international institution was designed to counter. 

 He gambled that the Western democracies would not go to war over the Rhineland, and he was right. 

 German generals had orders to retreat if France mobilised its army, yet France did nothing. 

 He gambled again over the annexation of Austria in March 1938 and the seizure of the Sudetenland following the Munich Agreement in September 1938, and once more the democracies chose appeasement over confrontation. 

 British Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain returned from Munich proclaiming "peace for our time," a phrase that would become a symbol of how badly the democracies had misjudged the situation. 

 The fundamental problem was not simply one of institutional design. It was a problem of political will. 

 Britain and France, the two democracies best placed to confront German expansion, were haunted by the memory of the First World War and deeply reluctant to risk another major conflict. 

 Their populations were weary of war and their economies were still recovering from the Great Depression, which meant that their military forces were not yet prepared for a new confrontation. 

 No League resolution or sanctions regime could have overcome this basic reluctance to act. 

 The League of Nations failed because the governments that created it were never willing to do what collective security demanded: to go to war in order to keep the peace. 

 When the United Nations replaced the League in 1945, its founders understood this lesson and gave the Security Council the power to authorise binding military action, a tool the League had never possessed.
